question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3},3{t}^{2}+4t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,-1⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,-1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =⟨c,-c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}=c \\ 6t+4=-c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2{t}^{2}.$ Substituting $c=2{t}^{2}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+4 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 2{t}^{2}+6t+4 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}+3t+2 & =0 \\ (t+2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the points corresponding to $t=-2$ and $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3},3(-1)^{2}+4(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{2}{3},-1⟩, \\ r(-2) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-2)^{3},3(-2)^{2}+4(-2)⟩=⟨-\frac{16}{3},4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-\frac{2}{3},-1)$ and $(-\frac{16}{3},4).$
